units.text: EXT. FLOODED RICE TERRACE - DUSK
Water the color of tin stands knee-deep across a stepped hillside, the stalks long since drowned.
Five people have been walking its dikes since the bridge went.
The sky is the same gray as the water, and the line between them has stopped meaning anything.
The oldest, a farmer named BAPAK SURYA, sixty-odd, leads along the narrow dike with a staff in one hand.
He tests each step before trusting it, and when the mud takes his foot to the ankle he does not curse, only pulls it free with a sound like a kiss and goes on.
Behind him comes his daughter-in-law, RATIH, thirty, a baby strapped to her chest in a sling made from a patterned cloth.
She walks with her chin tucked, shielding the child from the rain that has not yet started.
She does not speak.
Her lips move, counting something.
Third in line is the schoolteacher, MR. ARJUNA PERKASA, forty, still wearing his tie, soaked through.
He carries a transistor radio he cannot get to work and hasn't thrown away.
Every few steps he lifts it to his ear, shakes it, and lowers it again.
Fourth, a boy of twelve called GILANG, who is Ratih's brother.
He keeps to the edge, where the dike is thinnest, as if daring it.
He stops to pick up a drowned frog, studies it, and drops it back.
Then he runs three steps to catch up and nearly goes in.
Last, limping, is the stranger they picked up at the washed-out road, a woman in a field-medic's vest who has said only that her name is DEWI.
She walks with a hand pressed to her ribs.
Her eyes keep to the horizon in the way of someone who has decided to see the end of something.
At the next bend the dike widens into a little island with a lone coconut palm leaning on it.
Bapak Surya reaches it first, sets down his staff, and lowers himself onto a root.
He gestures with two fingers, and without a word the others gather.
Ratih unwraps the sling and sits, rocking the baby until it settles.
The teacher crouches beside her and sets the radio on his knee; he thumbs the dial slowly, and from it comes only a slow hiss.
The boy squats at the water's edge and cups his hands, drinks, and spits.
Dewi lowers herself last.
She takes her hand off her ribs, looks at it, and wipes it clean on the leg of her trousers.
The old man watches her do this.
He does not ask.
He takes a small packet of salted rice from his shirt and breaks it into five unequal portions, and the biggest, after a moment's thought, he gives to her.
She takes it.
She nods once.
Then she eats, slowly, while the first drops of rain begin to dimple the water around them.
